profile: machine learning: a unified algorithmic framework designed to identify computational models that accurately describe empirical data and the phenomena underlying it, with little or no human involvement.
classification: A machine learning task in which a computer is taught to distinguish between different classes or types of things, such as cats and dogs.

training set: A training set, also called training data, is a batch of examples used to train a computer or model. It is also typically referred to as a training set of data. It is the remaining portion of data used to train models. For example, a computer must be trained to recognize the difference between two types of animals by learning from such a batch.

feature engineering: Feature engineering comprises an array of techniques applied to data before they are used by either supervised or unsupervised models. It involves designing features so that models receive properly designed inputs, ideally with models finding or learning features themselves. In nonlinear cases, feature engineering determines the functional form of nonlinearities through human expertise.
generalization: the ability to apply what has been learned to new, previously unseen examples.

feature space: A feature space represents data items by feature values as coordinates; for example, each image in a training set can be represented in a two-dimensional feature space, where the features nose size and ear shape are the horizontal and vertical coordinate axes.
model training: the tuning of a set of parameters to a training set.

validation set: A random portion of data is removed to validate a model. It can be a batch of previously unseen images of cats and dogs, used to see how well the model identifies the animal in each image. This removed portion is commonly called validation data or validation set.
model validation: Model validation is the act of validating the efficacy of a trained learner by showing the computer a batch of previously unseen images.

nonlinear model: An array of nonlinear models can be trained and validated, with the hope that a more complex rule might better distinguish between cats and dogs. More generally, a general nonlinear model for regression and two-class classification is a weighted sum of B nonlinear functions: model(x, Θ) = w0 + f1(x)w1 + ... + fB(x)wB.

misclassification: Misclassification, also known as misidentification, occurs when an item is assigned a wrong label. A single dog (a Boston terrier) was misidentified. The error was due largely to the choice of features.

supervised learning: one of the two main categories of computational rules learned using machine learning, alongside unsupervised learning. It refers to the automatic learning of computational rules involving input/output relationships.

regression: Regression is a learning problem in which a model is fit to training data to make predictions about a continuous-valued output. It is one of two problem forms, along with classification, distinguished by the numerical form of the output. Linear regression fits a representative line or, in higher dimensions, a hyperplane to input/output data points. An example is predicting share price.
input/output relationship: In supervised learning, supervised learning problems refer to the automatic learning of computational rules involving input/output relationships.
continuous-valued output: A type of output whose values are continuous; share price is given as an example. Predictions about such an output can be made.

cost function: A cost function, also called a loss function, takes in a specific set of model parameters and returns a score indicating how well we would accomplish a given learning task using that choice of parameters.

mathematical optimization: In machine learning, optimization is the search for parameters of a learning model via well-defined mathematical functions. It is the study of computational methods for minimizing formal mathematical functions. Because these methods address the search for model parameters, the tools of mathematical optimization play a fundamental role throughout machine learning.

clustering: Clustering aims at identifying gross underlying structure in a set of input data by grouping together points that share some structural characteristic. Clustering techniques such as K-Means learn new representations to reduce the sheer number of points in a dataset.

model parameters: a specific set of values that serve as input to a procedure returning a score indicating how well a learning task would be accomplished. They can be internal parameters of a function, for example w(1)_0 and w(1)_1, and may be set randomly.

minimization: In machine learning, minimization is the process of reducing cost functions to find the ideal parameters of learning models. It is always pursued, as the aim is to minimize these cost functions.

cross-validation: a method for automating the setting of model capacity and optimization. Optimization plays a fundamental role in cross-validation, enabling the automatic learning of an appropriate nonlinear model for any dataset.
zero order optimization: a set of techniques also referred to as derivative free optimization techniques.

global minimum: A point w* such that g(w*) ≤ g(w) for all w. This zero-order definition captures the smallest function value. For a simple convex quadratic, the condition identifies the global minimum.
global maximum: a point w⋆ such that g(w⋆) ≥ g(w) for all w. This is the zero order definition of a global maximum.

local minimum: A point w⋆ is a local minimum if g(w⋆) ≤ g(w) for all w near w⋆. It is the smallest point with respect to its immediate neighbors. A point is a local or global minimum if ∂2/∂w2 g(v) > 0, since this occurs at convex portions of a function.

global optimization: a technique that evaluates the objective function at a large number of input points, then selects the input yielding the lowest function value as the approximate global minimizer.

aliases: zero order definitions for minima and maxima
profile: zero order optimality condition: a condition that packages together the zero order definitions for minima and maxima, collectively called optima. It is often referred to as the zero order condition for optimality.

local maximum: In zero-order optimization techniques, a local maximum is formally defined in the same way as a local minimum, with the inequality sign reversed from ≤ to ≥ in the zero-order condition.
random sampling: In zero-order optimization, random sampling picks the same number of input points at random.
uniform sampling: a technique for sampling (guessing) candidate points uniformly over an evenly spaced grid. This means the guesses are evenly spaced, and the sampling is uniform across the grid.
curse of dimensionality: generally speaking, it describes the exponential difficulty one encounters when trying to deal with functions of increasing input dimension.

descent direction: A descent direction is a direction vector in the input space that stems from a point w0 and points toward a new point w1 with a lower function evaluation. The first-order Taylor approximation, being a hyperplane, conveniently provides a descent direction, as used in gradient descent. Some optimization methods naturally determine high quality descent directions at a cost often cheaper than coordinate-wise approaches.

local optimization: a class of methods that work by starting with a single input point and then sequentially refining it, driving the point towards an approximate minimizer. Feature engineering and selection can drastically improve the efficacy of many local optimization methods. In feature learning, a run of local optimization may be made.

sequential refinement: an iterative approach that improves an initial estimate step by step. Local optimization methods refine the initial point sequentially, pulling it downhill to progressively lower function values. In clustering, the two-step process is repeated to refine centroids and clusters.
initial point: In zero-order optimization, an initial point is a sample input used as the starting point, denoted w0.

diminishing steplength rules: An alternative to fixed steplength rules, diminishing steplength rules shrink the steplength size at each step of local optimization. They are commonly used in local optimization. A simple example can compare fixed and diminishing steplength values.

random search: a zero-order optimization technique that finds a descent direction by sampling random directions from the current point, evaluating each candidate update, and selecting the one with the smallest function value if it is lower than the current point. Its parameters include steplength and maximum number of iterations, which are best chosen together.
convergence: In zero-order optimization, a small steplength combined with a large number of steps can guarantee convergence to a local minimizer.

coordinate descent: an optimization algorithm that examines one coordinate direction (and its negative) at a time, taking a step in that direction if it produces descent. Rather than collecting all coordinate directions and choosing a single best one, it steps immediately after examining each coordinate's positive and negative directions. This variant of coordinate search is much more effective at precisely the same computational cost. A related form of coordinate descent is especially effective when each per-coordinate equation can be solved in closed form.

coordinate search: a zero-order local optimization method. Along with descent algorithms, it addresses the inherent scaling issues of random local search by restricting the set of search directions to the coordinate axes of the input space.

steplength: Steplength, also called learning rate, is the size of the step used in local optimization and is associated with descent directions. A common alternative to fixed steplength rules is a diminishing steplength rule, which shrinks the size at each step. The same steplength may be used for multiple runs.

cost function history plot: a visualization used in optimization, named because the mathematical functions minimized in machine learning are often referred to as cost or loss functions. The notion is presented alongside descent directions, steplength/learning rates, and convergence.
first order optimization methods: local optimization algorithms that are some of the most popular techniques used to tackle machine learning problems.

gradient descent: an extremely popular local optimization algorithm that determines high quality descent directions. It is based on the first-order Taylor series approximation to a function. The algorithm uses a simple update step, employing the negative gradient as the descent direction. It is applied to minimize the Least Squares cost.

gradient: The first derivative of a function, generalized to multiple inputs. At a point, the derivative of a single-input function, or the gradient of a multi-input function, gives precisely the slope information at that point. Fundamental first-order optimization algorithms leverage the first derivative or gradient of a function.

automatic differentiation: a type of gradient calculator that automates the simple derivative rules for elementary functions and operations. Libraries such as autograd implement automatic differentiation and work with numpy; when using an automatic differentiator, functions should be expressed with autograd’s numpy wrapper.
chain rule: A rule for differentiation. It appears in the context of first-order optimization techniques. In a particular case, it is used to write d/dw g(w) as d/dw w^2 cos(w^2) = 2w cos(w^2).
numerical approximation: a variety of gradient calculator that provides numerical approximations, as distinct from calculators that automate simple derivative rules.

first order taylor series approximation: a line or hyperplane tangent to a function at its minimum point, also known as a first order Taylor approximation. A hyperplane in general is defined by w0 + x1w1 + x2w2 + ... + xNwN = y. As a hyperplane itself, this approximation conveniently provides a descent direction during gradient descent.

partial derivative: A partial derivative of a multivariable function is its derivative with respect to one variable while other variables are held constant. In first-order optimization, an N-dimensional point v where every partial derivative of g is zero is identified.
stationary points: Minima, maxima, and saddle points are collectively referred to as stationary or critical points of a function. The second derivative helps unveil the identity of stationary points.
first order system of equations: a system of N equations. It can be written compactly using gradient notation as ∇g(v) = 0.

saddle points: The first-order condition characterizes maxima and saddle points of non-convex functions. A saddle point is identified when the second derivative is zero and changes sign at that point.
closed form solution: a solution to equations that is found by solving the equations algebraically and can be written out on paper.

rayleigh quotient: a quantity closely related to the multi-input quadratic function and described as highly important alongside it. It appears in the context of first-order optimization techniques. Expressions can be written in the form of a Rayleigh quotient, as encountered in linear unsupervised learning.

convex quadratic function: A multi-input quadratic function of the form g(w) = a + b^T w + w^T C w, where C is an N x N symmetric matrix. The least squares cost function for linear regression is always a convex quadratic, and hence is a convex function.
symmetric linear system: A symmetric linear system is a system of equations of the form Cw = -1/2 b. It arises when setting an expression equal to zero.
momentum accelerated gradient descent: an optimization scheme named and described in the source material, presented within the context of first-order optimization techniques.
normalized gradient descent: an optimization scheme. It has a fully normalized form, and the standard and fully normalized schemes can be compared in the context of minimizing a function.
lipschitz continuous gradient: Functions g with Lipschitz continuous gradient satisfy ‖∇g(x) − ∇g(y)‖2 ≤ L‖x − y‖2.
second order optimality condition: This is the second order condition for optimality. It helps us better understand and quantify the behavior of Newton's method.
second order taylor series approximation: a concept in second order optimization techniques, related to the second order Taylor series expansion and the second order optimality condition.

convexity: A function g is said to be convex at v when its second derivative at v is nonnegative, i.e., g''(v) ≥ 0; it is concave when g''(v) ≤ 0. A convex function f has the property that the line segment connecting any two points on its graph always lies above the graph.
curvature: a notion defined by second derivatives. For a single-input function, curvature determines whether the function is convex or concave at a point via second derivative information.
positive semi-definite matrix: In second-order optimization techniques, the Hessian matrix itself is called positive semi-definite (or negative semi-definite).

quadratic function: A quadratic function can be multi-input. In the multi-input case, it is g(w) = a + b^T w + w^T C w. Its Hessian matrix is ∇2g(w) = 2C. This Hessian does not depend on w, so it is constant.
eigenvalues of the hessian: If all eigenvalues of ∇2g(v) are positive, then v is a local minimum.
first order condition for optimality: A condition used to compute the stationary point(s) of a quadratic function fairly easily.
newton's method: Newton's method is a second-order optimization technique with a simple implementation in Python.

regularized newton's method: a second-order optimization technique that uses a numerical stability/regularization parameter. In one described setting, the parameter is set to epsilon = 10^-7 to support numerical stability.

convergence criterion: A convergence criterion can take the form of a maximum iterations rule. In Newton-based second-order optimization, the potentially high computational cost of each step often incentivizes the use of more formal convergence criteria.
hessian matrix: an N × N matrix of second derivative information, requiring the storage and computation of the full second derivative matrix rather than only a gradient.
non-convex minimization: the task of finding a minimum of a non-convex function. Newton's method can behave very badly when applied to minimizing such functions.
second order optimization: optimization techniques that leverage both the first and second derivative(s) of a function in forming descent directions.
hessian-free optimization: in second-order optimization techniques, the latter set of adjustments is referred to as Hessian-free optimization.

eigenvalue decomposition: an alternative approach for checking that the eigenvalues of an N × N square symmetric matrix C, such as a Hessian matrix, are all non-negative. It is presented in the context of second-order optimization techniques.

second order definition of convexity: For a vector input function g(w), convexity is defined by checking the Hessian matrix ∇2g(w). The function is convex if, for every input w, all eigenvalues of ∇2g(w) are non-negative.
sub-sampled newton's step: A second-order optimization technique. In one implementation, it forms the Hessian approximation by ignoring all off-diagonal elements.
bfgs method: The Broyden–Fletcher–Goldfarb–Shanno (BFGS) method is an optimization technique. It is abbreviated as BFGS.
quasi-newton method: a secant-based method for computing a descent step; it uses an inverse.
secant method: The secant method employs the secant condition to derive a recursive update.
sherman-morrison identity: In second-order optimization, this identity is used to rewrite an update in terms of Fk.
least absolute deviations: a cost discussed in the context of linear regression, alongside least squares.

bias: The bias is the parameter w0 in a linear model, as in the line w0 + xw1 = y, where w0 is called the bias and w1 is the slope. In multi-class classification, the bias weight is separated from feature-touching weights: for the jth classifier the bias is b_j = w_{0,j}. Thus the bias term is the w0 component, distinct from the feature weights.

least squares cost function: a popular cost function that, for a given set of parameters in w, computes the total squared error between the associated hyperplane and the data. This quantity is also referred to as a least squares error measurement.
feature: Each dimension of the input is referred to as a feature or input feature in machine learning.

feature-touching weights: In linear regression, the parameters w1 through wN are called feature-touching weights, as each touches a corresponding input feature. The bias w0 is the only weight that does not touch a feature. Thus, in the linear model, all non-bias weights are associated with an individual input feature.

unconstrained optimization: an optimization problem with no constraints on the variables. Here, the goal is to minimize the average squared error between the linear prediction x_p^T w and the observed value y_p. The problem is stated as: minimize w (1/P) sum (x_p^T w - y_p)^2, where w is the variable vector and P is the number of terms.
normal equations: A term sometimes used in the context of least squares. Minimizing the least squares can be performed by solving its normal equations.
backtracking line search: an adjustable method. It tests values of α via an efficient bisection process, gradually decreasing α from an initial value until an inequality is satisfied.

vectorized implementation: A way to write numerical code by replacing explicit Python for loops with numerically equivalent operations from the numpy library. This approach removes much of the inefficiency of entry-wise Python loops. As a general rule, whenever vectorized implementations are available, one must avoid implementing algebraic expressions in Python using explicit for loops.

standard normalization: a very simple two-step procedure by which the input features of a dataset are first mean-centered and then re-scaled by the inverse of their standard deviation. It should be applied to the input features of a dataset prior to optimization. Using standard normalization to scale input is highly advantageous when employing gradient descent schemes.

multi-output regression: a regression problem with multiple outputs. Nonlinear feature engineering can be applied, and a key design choice is whether to model each output separately with a nonlinear model per output, or jointly with a single nonlinear model that predicts all outputs simultaneously. Multi-output regression was introduced in the context of linear regression.
convex combination: a point between x and y, characterized by λx + (1 − λ)y for a certain λ ∈ (0, 1).
non-negative eigenvalues: In linear regression, the eigenvalues of such a matrix are always non-negative. This property means every eigenvalue is greater than or equal to zero.
quadratic cost function: a cost function of the form g(w) = a + b^T w + w^T C w, which is a general quadratic in w. It has a constant term, a linear term in w, and a quadratic term in w.
inner product: An inner product is symmetric, so its two arguments can be interchanged without changing the value. Consequently, inner products can be switched around in algebraic manipulations.
outer product: an operation that forms a matrix. In linear regression, the matrix C is constructed from a sum of outer product matrices.
eigenvalues: In linear regression, the eigenvalues of such a matrix are always non-negative.
perceptron cost: a cost function also known as the rectified linear unit (ReLU) cost and the hinge cost. It can be averaged over the entire dataset to form a proper cost function.
softmax approximation to max: a generic smooth approximation to the max function, given by log(e^{s0} + ... + e^{s_{C-1}}) for any C scalar values s0,...,s_{C-1}.
rectified linear unit: The functional form max(0, ·) is often called a rectified linear unit for historical reasons. It describes a point-wise cost in linear two-class classification.
convex cost function: a cost function that is always convex but has only a single discontinuous derivative in each input dimension.
point-wise cost: a per-sample cost in linear two-class classification, defined for sample p as gp(w) = max(0, -yp x_p^T w). It is zero when yp x_p^T w >= 0 and positive otherwise.

trivial solution: In the Perceptron cost, the trivial solution is the zero-weight solution at w = 0. The cost always has this solution, since g(0) = 0; therefore, in practice one may need to take care to avoid finding it.
softmax cost: an overall cost function for linear two-class classification, given by g(w) = \sum_p \log(1 + e^{-y_p x_p^T w}), where y_p is the label and x_p is the feature vector for data point p.
weight divergence to infinity: In linear two-class classification, the Softmax cost decreases, and its minimum is achieved only as the parameter C tends to infinity.

numerical instability: a condition in which local optimization schemes can experience severe numerical instability when they make large progress at each step. This can arise in the context of linear two-class classification.

early stopping: a regularization strategy for tuning high-capacity models. It is straightforward and requires only slight adjustments to the typical use of local optimization. In practice, one makes a run of local optimization, tuning all model parameters, and then uses the set of weights from that run at which the model achieves minimum validation error.

regularization: A complementary approach to feature selection. Instead of building up a model from the bottom, regularization takes a top-down view: it starts with a complete model that includes all input features and gradually removes features of inferior importance. This top-down approach is generally referred to in machine learning jargon as a regularization strategy. A related term is regularizer-based regularization. Along with boosting, regularization is one of two popular ways for performing feature selection.

normal vector to hyperplane: In linear two-class classification, the feature-touching weights ω define the normal vector of the linear decision boundary. The normal vector to a hyperplane is always perpendicular to the hyperplane.

signed distance to decision boundary: For a point x_p, the signed distance d to the decision boundary is d = (b + x_p^T ω) / ||ω||_2. This value is a measure of confidence in how the point should be labeled in two-class classification.

weight normalization: rescales a linear classifier's weight vector by dividing the weights by the magnitude of the weight vector. In two-class linear classification, this gives a consistent way to normalize the weights. In multi-class classification, each linear classifier's weights are normalized by the length of its normal vector, which contains all feature-touching weights.

regularization parameter: The regularization parameter λ is always non-negative (λ ≥ 0). It balances the trade-off between the cost and regularizer, controlling the mixture of the two and determining how strongly one term is pressured relative to the other. In linear two-class classification and feature learning, λ is referred to as the regularization parameter.

l2 regularizer: the term ∥ω∥2^2, referred to as a regularizer. It can be added to a cost function. In kernel methods, when the sum is kernelized, the kernelized form is the sum of the kernelized cost and regularizer.
regularized softmax cost: a relaxed problem formulation in which the cost function is a linear combination of the original softmax cost and the magnitude of the feature weights.
constrained softmax cost: a cost for linear two-class classification, defined by minimizing (1/P) Σ log(1 + e^{-y_p(b + x_p^T ω)}) subject to ∥ω∥_2^2 = 1.

margin of separating hyperplane: For a separating hyperplane, the margin is the width of the buffer zone confined between two evenly spaced translates of the hyperplane that just touch each respective class. The margin length is the distance between those evenly spaced translates, and it serves as a reasonable standard for judging the quality of such hyperplanes.

margin-perceptron cost: a cost function for linear two-class classification, written g(w) = Σ max(0, 1 − y_p x̌_p^T w). It sums over training examples p the amount by which the margin y_p x̌_p^T w falls below 1; the max(0, ·) term contributes zero when the margin is at least 1 and becomes positive when the margin is below 1.

smoothed margin-perceptron: A variant of the Margin-Perceptron in linear two-class classification, obtained by replacing the max operator with softmax. The smoothed expression is log(1 + e^{1 - y_p x̌^T w}).
maximum margin decision boundary: In linear two-class classification, the decision boundary with the maximum margin is intuitively the best choice.

hard-margin svm: In linear two-class classification, the hard-margin SVM minimizes ∥ω∥2^2 subject to max(0, 1 − yp(b + xp^Tω)) = 0 for each training sample p. This constraint forces the hinge term to zero and is equivalent to yp(b + xp^Tω) ≥ 1, i.e. every sample has a margin of at least 1.

aliases: margin as 2 over norm of omega
profile: margin computation via normal vector: the margin is computed as the L2 distance between the two support hyperplanes, expressed as 2 divided by the norm of the normal vector omega. Because this distance equals 2 divided by the norm, finding the separating hyperplane with maximum margin is equivalent to finding the one with the smallest possible normal vector omega.
soft-margin support vector machine: a regularized form of the Margin-Perceptron cost function, also referred to as a squared margin SVM.

support vectors: In SVM linear two-class classification, support vectors are points from both classes that are equidistant from the linear decision boundary; translates of the decision boundary pass through these points.
log-loss svm: A term sometimes used for the soft-margin SVM cost function.
categorical cross entropy cost: a cost function that is derived and is equivalent to the cross entropy cost. It is referred to as the categorical cross entropy cost function.

one-hot encoded labels: one-hot encoding transforms original numerical label values, such as binary labels (yp in {0,1}), into one-hot encoded vectors. It is also a method of encoding categorical features, sometimes referred to as one-hot encoding.
log error cost: A cost function employed in linear two-class classification. It is preferred because it better incentivizes learning by producing a convex cost function.
confidence scoring: In linear two-class classification, once a proper decision boundary is learned, the confidence in any point is judged based on the point's distance to the decision boundary.

classification accuracy: a measure, denoted A, for a trained model. It is the percentage of the training dataset whose labels are correctly predicted by the model. This measure gives a simple way to quantify how well the model's predicted labels match the true labels on the training data. Accuracy is expressed as a percentage.

misclassification count: the number of misclassifications that a fully trained model produces over its training dataset. It is called the simplest metric for judging the quality of a fully trained model, obtained by counting those errors.
step function approximation: In linear two-class classification, classification cost functions are ultimately based on smooth approximations to a discrete step function.

early stopping by validation accuracy: a stopping rule that picks the training step with the best classification result. In linear two-class classification, the best step and corresponding weights are those with the lowest number of misclassifications (or likewise the highest accuracy), not the lowest cost function value.

cost function versus misclassification discrepancy: A decreasing cost function value does not guarantee a decrease in the number of misclassifications. Cost value and misclassification count can therefore diverge during optimization: the two measure different criteria, so a lower cost does not by itself indicate better classification performance.
balanced accuracy: a combined metric obtained by averaging two metrics. It is introduced in the context of linear two-class classification and extended to the multi-class setting.
confusion matrix: a simple look-up table used in classification that breaks down results by actual class membership (rows) and predicted class membership (columns).
precision: In machine learning jargon, precision is an individual accuracy metric, also called A+1. It is paired with specificity, also called A−1.

weighted classification: A method in linear two-class classification where individual data points are assigned weights to emphasize or de-emphasize their importance to the classification model. This is enabled by the fact that two-class classification cost functions are summable over individual points, allowing point-wise weighting as in regression.

weighted softmax cost: a cost function that arises from weighting two-class cost functions, specifically the Softmax cost. A general weighted version of the two-class Softmax cost exists, and the analogous weighted multi-class Softmax cost is considered.
point-wise weights: In linear two-class classification, the values β1, β2, ..., βP are fixed point-wise weights.
weighting by confidence: assigning fixed weight values based on one's confidence in the legitimacy of a datapoint.

inverse class frequency weighting: a technique in classification where class weights are set inversely proportional to the number of members of each class. It is common to assign such weights in linear two-class classification.
linear multi-class classification: a method for dealing with multi-class classification settings by generalizing prior linear classification approaches.
multi-class perceptron: A perspective on multi-class classification, discussed alongside one-versus-all as one of several approaches.
categorical multi-class classification: an extension of basic principles in linear multi-class classification, alongside weighted multi-class classification.
weighted multi-class classification: an extension of basic classification principles, listed alongside categorical multi-class classification in the context of linear multi-class classification.

one-versus-all classification: a multi-class classification strategy that learns C two-class classifiers over the entire dataset, with the cth classifier trained to distinguish the cth class from the remainder of the data. This approach is also called one-versus-rest. It can also be applied to tune individual columns of a weight matrix one at a time.

fusion rule: In multi-class classification, the fusion rule is a decision rule that fuses C two-class classifiers together to determine the label assigned to a point, based on signed distance to decision boundary. In nonlinear feature engineering, one aims to tune the parameters of W to satisfy the fusion rule.

piecewise linear decision boundary: A decision boundary made up of linear segments. In general, when using linear two-class classifiers, the boundary resulting from the fusion rule is always piecewise linear.

mini-batch gradient descent: an extension of standard gradient descent designed to accelerate minimization of cost functions consisting of a sum of P terms. Example settings include a learning rate of α = 10−2, batch size 200, and 20 steps/epochs applied to a multi-class Softmax cost. Empirically, a mini-batch run drastically accelerates minimization in terms of both the cost function and the number of misclassifications.

softmax cost function: A cost function for multi-class classification, also referred to as cross entropy cost. It is minimized when training linear multi-class classifiers, and a two-class version can be used to learn a separator. The multi-class softmax cost averages a log-sum-exp term minus the linear response of the true class over data points; the two-class softmax cost has the form Σ log(1 + e^{-y_p(b + f_p^T ω)}). It is also among the cost functions used in feature learning.

multi-class perceptron cost: a cost function used in linear multi-class classification. It is an objective that can be minimized, as can cross entropy/softmax cost functions, when training a linear multi-class classifier.
multi-class classification metrics: metrics used for evaluating multi-class classification problems. They are natural extensions of the metrics first described for two-class problems.
batch size: In the mini-batch version, a batch of size 200 is used.
categorical labels: Categorical labels are a choice for label values that is inherently arbitrary; they are described as the most arbitrary such choice.
class imbalance: a situation in classification where classes are not equally represented. It can be dealt with by adjusting the weights of the cost function.
convexity of cost functions: For linear multi-class classification, the multi-class Perceptron and Softmax costs are always convex, regardless of the dataset used.

hessian of softmax cost: The Hessian of the multi-class Softmax cost function can be computed block-wise. This Hessian is a matrix of second-order partial derivatives. In the setting of linear multi-class classification, the second derivatives are organized in blocks when computing the Hessian.

spanning set: a set of vectors, drawn as arrows, that are particular points in a space. It is often called a basis; it is the set of vectors over which we aim to represent every other point in the space.

mean-centering: a simple and completely reversible operation that involves subtracting off the mean of the dataset along each input dimension, so that the dataset straddles the origin. It applies to N-dimensional input datapoints.
orthonormal spanning set: a very special kind of spanning set whose elements have unit length and are perpendicular or orthogonal to each other; also known as an orthonormal basis.
autoencoder formula: expresses how a point xp is first encoded via wp = CT xp and then decoded back to itself as Cwp = CCT xp.
projection: In linear algebra, a projection maps a vector onto a subspace. In this context, the decoding Cwp is precisely the projection of xp onto the subspace spanned by C.

linear autoencoder: A linear autoencoder has a least squares cost function, which can be thought of as enforcing the autoencoder formula when properly minimized. Because of this least squares formulation, it is often referred to as the linear autoencoder.

principal component analysis: Principal component analysis, or PCA for short, is a method used in practice. When PCA is applied to reduce the dimension of a dataset, it does so by learning a new, smaller set of features. This new set of features is one over which the dataset may be fairly represented.
dimension reduction: PCA can be used to reduce the dimension of data in predictive modeling. Feature selection can be thought of as a supervised dimension reduction technique.
covariance matrix regularization: replacing the raw covariance matrix with the regularized form 1/P X X^T + λ I_{N×N} to avoid computational trouble when computing principal components.
k-means clustering: an elementary example of clustering algorithms, which are unsupervised learning methods.

matrix factorization: a linear representation model based on the assumption that some ideal spanning set of K fundamental taste vectors exists, allowing these vectors to be packaged as an N × K matrix C. The goal is for each data vector x_p to be truly expressed as a linear combination of those columns, i.e. C w_p ≈ x_p.

concept_name: least squares cost for incomplete data
aliases: least squares cost for incomplete data
profile: least squares cost for incomplete data: a cost function for incomplete data, defined as g(w1,...,wP, C) = 1/P ∑_p ||{C w_p - x_p}|_{Ω_p}||^2. It minimizes the least squares cost only over the entries indexed by Ω_p, rather than over all entries. The expression {C w_p - x_p}|_{Ω_p} restricts the residual to the components in Ω_p for each data point p.
cluster centroid: A cluster center is also called a centroid. Each cluster centroid is marked by a star symbol.

cluster assignment: The process of assigning a data point x_p to a cluster. It is defined by the condition that x_p belongs to cluster k⋆ when a_p equals the argument minimizing the squared Euclidean distance between x_p and cluster centers c_k. Therefore, the selected cluster is the one with the nearest centroid.
centroid initialization: selecting starting locations for K centroids; one way is to start with a random guess at the locations of the K centroids.

intra-cluster distance: A metric for determining the best clustering from a set of runs. It is defined as the average distance of each point to its assigned cluster centroid. The term is synonymous with 'average intra-cluster distance.'
scree plot: In machine learning, a scree plot is a plot of the best distance value attained for each value of K tried. This plot is often referred to as a scree plot in machine learning jargon.

non-negative matrix factorization: a matrix factorization problem in which a matrix X is approximated as the product C W, with both C and W constrained to be non-negative. The objective is to minimize the squared Frobenius norm of the residual, ||C W - X||_F^2, subject to C ≥ 0 and W ≥ 0.
sparse coding: Sparse coding is a constrained matrix factorization problem, often written as minimize ∥CW − X∥_F^2 subject to ∥wp∥_0 ≤ S, p = 1, . . . , P.
pca least squares cost: The PCA least squares cost function is not convex; it is bi-convex.
alternating minimization: an optimization approach widely used to solve general matrix factorization problems.

bi-convex function: A bi-convex function is convex in each matrix of parameters C and W independently. When one parameter matrix is held fixed, the function is convex with respect to the other matrix.
orthogonal matrix: a matrix V, also called an orthonormal matrix, satisfies V V^T = I. This holds when the eigenvectors are all perpendicular to each other, making V an orthonormal matrix.
variance maximization: In linear unsupervised learning, variance maximization aims to recover a basis vector c1 that points in the maximum direction of variance in the dataset.

feature selection: can be thought of as a supervised dimension reduction technique that reduces the total number of features involved in a regression or classification, making the resulting model more human interpretable.

boosting: Boosting, also called forward stagewise selection, is a popular bottom-up feature-selection approach. It gradually builds a model one feature at a time by training a supervised learner sequentially, one weight at a time. Boosting builds up a single cross-validated model by gradually adding simple models consisting of a single universal approximator unit. It is presented as one of two popular feature-selection methods, alongside regularization.
histogram features: a common feature engineering tool, namely the histogram feature transformation, used for a variety of data types including categorical, text, image, and audio data.
inner product similarity: The inner product between two BoW vectors always ranges between 0 and 1 and may be used as a rough geometric measure of similarity.
normalization: In feature engineering, each BoW vector is normalized to have unit length.
stemming: Stemming is a preprocessing step that reduces related words with a common stem or root to their common linguistic root and represents them by that root.
stop words: uninformative words such as 'are' and 'the'.
discriminative features: Features that help distinguish between classes are discriminative. However, raw pixel values are typically not discriminative enough to be useful for machine learning tasks.

edge histogram features: a method for summarizing an image's edge content by creating a normalized histogram of that content. For each image, a histogram is constructed from its edge information and then normalized. The simple edge histogram concept can be generalized, and such generalizations are widely used as feature transformations for visual object recognition.
spectrogram: a feature transformation for audio that computes frequency histograms over overlapping windows, producing a feature vector; common in speech recognition.
nonlinear feature engineering: a concept in the context of supervised and unsupervised learning.
nonlinear regression: a general framework for modeling nonlinear relationships by engineering nonlinear feature transformations.
transformed feature space: A feature space resulting from nonlinear feature engineering, in which a tuned nonlinear model becomes a linear one.
non-convex cost function: in nonlinear feature engineering, the associated cost functions are generally non-convex.
decision boundary: The decision boundary consists of all inputs x where f^T w = 0.
feature sharing: the practice of choosing a single set of nonlinear feature transformations and sharing them among all C two-class models.
degree two polynomial expansion: the full degree two polynomial expansion of the input, consisting of features of the form x_1^i x_2^j where i + j ≤ 2.
manifold: A manifold is a nonlinear surface.
encoder-decoder composition: a model that applies an encoder function fe followed by a decoder function fd, expressed as model(x, Θ) = fd(fe(x)).

output transformation: To produce a linear relationship, one will have to transform the output (response) variable rather than the input. This approach is also called response transformation or output linearization.
nonlinear classification: a two-class classification task, also called nonlinear two-class classification.
kernel pca: a more restricted version of nonlinear PCA, often termed kernel principal component analysis.
kernel k-means: an extension of K-means clustering to a nonlinear setting.

standard basis vector constraint: a constraint that each weight vector wp is a standard basis vector from the set {e_k} for k=1..K. A standard basis vector has exactly one entry equal to 1 and all other entries 0.
feature learning: Feature learning, also called automatic feature engineering, automates the feature engineering task and learns proper features directly from the data itself.

universal approximators: manageable collections of relatively simple nonlinear functions that serve as fundamental building blocks of an infinitude. They are part of a first step in organizing the pursuit of automation by grouping such building blocks into practical sets. Three popularly used strains are fixed-shape approximators, artificial neural networks, and trees.
linear combination: A linear combination f1w1 + f2w2 + ... + fBwB = y defines a new N-dimensional vector.
training error: a measurement tool that indicates how well a tuned model fits the training data; it does not indicate when the tuned model becomes too complex.

overfitting: Overfitting begins when a highly complex model fits the given data extremely well, at the cost of not representing the underlying phenomenon well. This language is used because such models prioritize fitting the data over capturing the underlying relationship. The term thus indicates a trade-off between matching observed data and representing the real-world phenomenon.
underfitting: A tuned model underfits when it does not fit the given data well.

model complexity: Model complexity refers to how 'wiggly' a tuned model fit is. We only control complexity indirectly by how we set both capacity and optimization dials. Therefore, the complexity of a tuned model is not directly adjustable; it is determined by capacity and optimization settings, and it reflects the behavior of the tuned fit.
optimization dial: a control that, together with the capacity dial, indirectly sets the complexity of a tuned model. Complexity roughly corresponds to how 'wiggly' the model fit is.
validation error: the error computed on validation data. In model selection, the model with the lowest validation error is deemed the best choice from a set of trained models.
high capacity model: The term appears. No definition is provided.
regularizer: A regularizer is a simple function that can be added to a machine learning cost.
regularized cost function: a cost function that incorporates a regularization term as a linear combination of a base cost g(Θ) and a penalty h(Θ), weighted by a coefficient λ, giving g(Θ)+λh(Θ).
l2 regularization based cross-validation: a method in which the appropriate tuning of each model’s parameters is achieved via l2 regularization and cross-validation.
ensembling: In machine learning, an ensembling method refers to any method of combining different models.
k-folds cross-validation: A cross-validation method that selects a single model with minimum average validation error over all splits together.
sparse feature selection: a process commonly used to produce high performing and human-interpretable results.

model capacity: refers to the range of shapes a function can take, given all different settings of its internal parameters. The capacity of each single layer unit can be roughly illustrated. For a model built with units of a universal approximator, capacity must be properly set.
fixed-shape universal approximators: collections of various nonlinear features which have no internal (tunable) parameters.
fourier basis: a set of paired sine and cosine waves with ever-increasing frequency, of the form f_{2m-1}(x)=sin(2πmx) and f_{2m}(x)=cos(2πmx).

exponential scaling of fixed-shape units: In kernel methods, the number of units of a typical fixed-shape approximator in a model employing a complete package of such units grows exponentially with the dimension of input.

complete package of fixed-shape units: In kernel methods, this term denotes using all polynomial units of a given degree together as a set. Polynomial units are virtually always used as a complete package of a certain degree, not individually.
kernel trick: a concept motivated by a serious scaling issue.

concept_name: weight vector decomposition over feature matrix
aliases: weight vector decomposition over feature matrix
decomposition of ω over columns of f
profile: weight vector decomposition over feature matrix: In an M-dimensional space, any vector ω can be decomposed over the column space of a given feature matrix F as ω = Fz + r. The term Fz lies in the column space of F, while r is a residual vector. This decomposition splits a weight vector into a part spanned by the feature matrix columns and a remaining part.
orthogonal component r: In the context of kernel methods, r is orthogonal to a subspace. Its key property is being perpendicular to that subspace.
kernel matrix: A kernel matrix is a symmetric P × P matrix H = FTF, referred to simply as a kernel for short.
kernelization via weight vector substitution: in kernel methods, this technique substitutes a representation of the weight vector ω back into the cost function.
kernelized least squares: the function g(b, z) = Σ_p (b + h_p^T z - y_p)^2.
kernelized logistic regression: a kernelized form of the Softmax.
entry-wise kernel matrix construction: The kernel matrix may be constructed entry-wise via simple formulae.
polynomial kernel: A polynomial kernel can be defined entry-wise, in a similar manner, for general N and D. It appears in the context of kernel methods.
kernelized l2 regularizer: In the kernelized form of the regularized least squares problem, the regularizer is expressed as λ z^T H z.

kernelized squared margin: a squared-margin/soft-margin SVM cost in kernel methods. It evaluates a sum over data points of squared hinge terms, max(0, 1 - y_p(b + h^T z_p))^2. This is the squared margin form of soft-margin support vector machines.

kernelized multi-class softmax: a kernel-based variant of the standard multi-class softmax approach. It is described in the context of kernel methods, indicating that kernel techniques are applied to the multi-class softmax formulation.
naive cross-validation: a cross-validation approach that simply performs a raw search over various models.
regularization-based cross-validation: cross-validation via regularization with the l2 norm. It is common practice when employing polynomial and Fourier kernels.
fourier kernel: The Fourier kernel for vector-valued input appears in the context of kernel methods. It is used to calculate the corresponding i,jth entry of the kernel matrix.
fully-connected neural network: a general multi-layer neural network, also referred to as a fully-connected network, multi-layer perceptron, and deep feedforward neural network.
activation function: a nonlinear function applied to a linear combination of inputs. It is typically an elementary mathematical function such as tanh, ReLU, or logistic sigmoid.
single-layer unit: A shorthand term for a single hidden-layer unit, as used in the context of fully-connected neural networks.

recursive construction: a manner of writing out a function as a recursive recipe for creating single-layer network units. It emphasizes the recursive nature of constructing two-layer units using single-layer ones.

hidden layer: In a visual depiction of a neural network model, the hidden layer appears in the middle, where blue circles representing all U1 activations align. The hidden layer is therefore associated with these activations.
neural network architecture: A visual representation of a neural network is often referred to as a neural network architecture, or simply an architecture.
input layer: The layer of a neural network into which input data is injected, also often referred to as the first layer. It is 'visible' because we can see the data we feed into the network.

output layer: The output layer is the final layer of a neural network and is often called the final layer. It is the layer that corresponds to the model's final output. Unlike hidden layers, the output layer is visible to us.

weight matrix: A weight matrix is a parameter matrix formed by arranging each unit's parameters into a column vector, starting with the bias and then the input-touching weights. These column vectors become the columns of an (N + 1) × U1 matrix. This internal weight matrix W1 is defined for single-layer units.

vector activation: a vector function that takes a d × 1 vector v and returns a vector of the same size containing the activation of each of its input's entries. Thus the operation is element-wise and the output has the same size as the input.

two-layer unit: a short term for a two-hidden-layer neural network unit. The term is used when creating such a unit, introduced as a concise alternative to the fuller name. In this context, a two-layer unit denotes a unit with two hidden layers.
step function: A step function is a function that takes on just two values: 0 (off) and 1 (on).

vanishing gradient problem: a technical issue in neural networks where gradients of a network employing sigmoid activations shrink undesirably, preventing proper parameter tuning. The problem balloons as more hidden layers are added.

sigmoid activation: The logistic sigmoid can be used as an activation function. It was viewed as a reasonable compromise between the desired neuronal model and the practical need to tune parameters properly. When used as an activation function, it often leads to a technical issue called the vanishing gradient problem.
backpropagation: The backpropagation algorithm, often referred to simply as backpropagation or backprop for short.
maxout activation: an activation function defined as a(x) = max(v0 + v1x, w0 + w1x), taking the maximum of two linear functions of the input.
batch normalization: A step grafted onto a hidden layer of a neural network. It keeps the distribution of that unit normalized whenever network parameters change during optimization.
internal covariate shift: the constant alteration of these distributions, also called covariate shift for short.
split point: A split point is a parameter, denoted s, that defines the boundary between the two levels.
stump: The stump is the most basic tree-based universal approximator. It is a simple step function.
bagging: A technique that combines multiple cross-validated models to produce a single higher-performing model.
leaf parameters: In tree-based learners, leaf parameters—also called step levels—are the two values denoted by v1 and v2.
growing of a tree: in machine learning, a recursive procedure often referred to by this term in the field's jargon.
local function approximator: Tree-based universal approximators are sometimes called local function approximators.
regression tree: a general tree-based universal approximator used for the problem of regression.
addition of trees: deeper, more flexible trees can be constructed via addition of shallower trees.
staircase-like cost: In tree-based learners, the cost function can create highly non-convex, staircase-like functions.
human interpretability: Shallow tree-based units are often easy to interpret by humans.

mid-point split point: In tree-based learners, a split point chosen as the mid-point of a flat region. Only one split point per flat region needs to be tested, and the mid-point is used as that single test point.
candidate split points: values created by recording every mid-point between input data points; these candidate split point values are used as potential split locations in tree-based learners.
optimal leaf values: In tree-based learners, the optimal leaf values v⋆_L and v⋆_R are assigned to the left and right leaves, respectively, and equal the mean of the output.
leaf-value optimization: in tree-based learners, optimizing the leaf values of a function using an appropriate cost function.
tree-based learner: a model that can dispense with bias and weights.
residual fitting: in tree-based learners, an approach interpreted as successive rounds of fitting to the residual.
feature subsampling: a technique in tree-based learners in which only a random subset of feature dimensions is sampled for viable split points.
recursively defined trees: regression and classification trees that are defined recursively.
computational trade-off: in tree-based learning, the contrast between training a large number of fully grown trees and training a smaller number of cross-validated trees.
mode: the most frequent classification result among multiple decision trees; used to combine their predictions into a final output, e.g., taking the mode of five classification trees.
pruning: Pruning is a tree-specific form of regularization that is based on cross-validation.
gradient boosting: Gradient boosting is a specific application of boosting, based on cross-validation, to tree-based learners.
random forests: a specialized application of bagging to tree-based learners.

classification trees: recursively defined models for classification. Unless human interpretability of the final model is of primary concern, one virtually never uses a single classification tree, but a bagged ensemble of them.
